subject: 🤖 AI job casualties

Plus: Labor market resilience | Tuesday, November 03, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 03, 2026

🗳️ Americans head to the polls with affordability concerns looming large over the midterm elections. Follow Axios.com tonight for election results and analysis.

  • In today's Macro: early signs of AI's toll on laid-off workers. Plus, a strong reading on job openings and hiring as the first major data for October looms.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 901 words, a 3.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: AI job displacement is looking extra painful
 

Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios
 

AI may be repeating a painful pattern from previous technological revolutions: Workers who lose their jobs because of the technology struggle to find employment and risk displacement all over again.

Why it matters: AI does not need to trigger mass layoffs to cause lasting damage.

  • Against the "low-hire, low-fire" backdrop, workers whose skills become obsolete could struggle to find new jobs and suffer years of lost earnings — even if the broader economy avoids a major rise in unemployment.

What they're saying: Workers displaced by earlier technological shifts — including personal computers and industrial automation — often ended up in less-skilled jobs as demand for their expertise faded, Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei wrote in a new note.

  • "We see early signs of a similar pattern today," Mei wrote.

By the numbers: Workers most likely displaced by AI in 2025 took roughly a month longer to find new employment than other laid-off workers, according to Mei's analysis of more than 15,000 workers who lost jobs between 2016 and 2025.

  • There's no definitive count of how many workers have lost jobs to AI. The research instead estimates which layoffs were most likely AI-related — based on workers' occupations, industry AI adoption rates and the circumstances, such as whether their positions were eliminated.
  • Those workers were roughly 10 percentage points more likely to remain unemployed a year after losing their jobs.
  • Among displaced workers from AI-exposed jobs who found new work in 2025, roughly three-quarters landed in occupations with similar or greater AI exposure — up from just over half in 2023.

The big picture: AI could eventually create new kinds of jobs, but those opportunities may take years to materialize.

Between the lines: Older workers are especially vulnerable to AI-related employment disruption.

  • Then. A Goldman Sachs analysis from earlier this year, looking at three decades of job losses, found that workers over age 55 displaced from declining occupations suffered earnings losses exceeding 10% when they found new full-time work. Those under 35 saw almost no losses.
  • Now. Workers under 35 most likely displaced by AI took about three weeks longer to find full-time jobs than other laid-off workers their age. For those 35 and older, that gap was five weeks.

What to watch: Young college graduates are struggling to get hired, raising the possibility that AI is replacing some of the entry-level work that once launched their careers.

  • Recent graduates' unemployment rate averaged 5.4% in the third quarter, compared with 4% for all workers, according to Federal Reserve Bank of New York data updated yesterday. That gap has roughly doubled since 2019.
  • Underemployment is also rising: About 42% of employed recent graduates held jobs that don't require a degree, up a percentage point from before the pandemic.

The bottom line: Technological revolutions have made the economy more prosperous but left some workers permanently worse off. AI risks repeating that pattern.

2. Strong September job openings and hiring
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Employers posted more job openings and hired more workers in September, in a new sign that the overall labor market remains resilient, AI-related job losses notwithstanding.

The big picture: Every major component of the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey report, which gives the richest data on what is happening to the labor market beneath the headline numbers, pointed to conditions improving in September.

  • The October employment report is due out Friday, and analysts expect it to confirm solid job growth and a low, steady unemployment rate at the onset of autumn.

By the numbers: The number of job openings rose by 333,000 in September, pushing the rate of openings to its highest since April. The number of hires was up by 131,000, pushing the hiring rate up a tick as well.

  • Also pointing to solid labor market conditions: The number of people voluntarily quitting their jobs — a sign of confidence in their ability to find a new position — rose by 321,000. That pushed the quits rate up two-tenths to 2.1%, its highest since June 2025.
  • The number of layoffs and discharges fell by 127,000, bringing the rate at which people involuntarily lost their jobs to 1%, remaining near historic lows.

The intrigue: The industry breakdowns show that job opportunities vary significantly across sectors, with blue-collar sectors looking better than many predominantly office-based sectors.

  • The rate of job openings in manufacturing rose 0.4 percentage point, as did the rate of openings in the construction sector and in transportation, warehousing and utilities.
  • By contrast, the rate of openings in finance and insurance fell 0.5 percentage point, and federal government openings were down 0.4 point.
  • The pattern wasn't uniform, however, as opening rates climbed for both the information and professional and business services sectors.

State of play: Taken together, the JOLTS data paints a picture of a labor market that is holding up quite well despite various headwinds, including AI-related productivity gains and spiking energy prices due to the Iran war.

  • It supports the view held by Federal Reserve leadership that the labor market is basically holding up fine and that more attention should be on inflation trends at this moment.
